message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. These are derived from the Texas Property Code (Title 2, Chapter 91) and related statutes. If you need more detailed guidance—especially if your situation involves a lease dispute, landlord harassment, or a specific legal issue—consider consulting a local attorney or tenant‑rights organization. | Area | What the law says | Practical take‑away | |------|-------------------|---------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **$1,000** for a single‑unit dwelling.
• For multi‑unit buildings, the limit is **$2,000**.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after the lease ends, unless the landlord gives a written statement of deductions. | Keep a copy of the receipt and any written agreement on the deposit amount. | | **Lease Terms** | • Written leases are not required, but a written lease is strongly recommended because it protects both parties.
• A lease must contain the rent amount, due date, and the landlord’s name. | Get everything in writing—even verbal agreements can be hard to enforce. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords cannot raise rent during a fixed‑term lease unless the lease allows it.
• For month‑to‑month tenants, landlords must give **30 days’ written notice** before raising rent. | If you’re on a month‑to‑month lease, expect a 30‑day notice before any increase. | | **Habitability** | • Landlords must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition and maintain essential services (heat, hot water, plumbing, electrical).
• Failure to do so can be grounds for withholding rent or terminating the lease. | Document any maintenance issues with photos and written notices. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | Ask for a written notice of entry; keep a log of all entries. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the formal eviction procedure: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days for nonpayment) or a **Notice to Cure or Quit** (10 days for lease violations).
• After the notice period, the landlord files an unlawful detainer action in court. | Do not ignore notices; respond promptly or seek legal advice. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the federal Fair Housing Act and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | Report discriminatory practices to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Retaliation** | • Landlords cannot retaliate against tenants who exercise their legal rights (e.g., filing a complaint about habitability). | Keep records of any complaints and subsequent actions taken by the landlord. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Tenants have the right to use the property without unreasonable interference. | Document any disturbances or intrusions. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Tenants may sublet or assign the lease only with the landlord’s written consent, which cannot be unreasonably withheld. | Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Tenants can sue for unpaid rent, damages, or breach of contract.
• Courts may award actual damages, statutory damages, or attorney’s fees. | Preserve receipts, correspondence, and any evidence of damages. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Get a written lease** – even if you’re on a month‑to‑month arrangement. 2. **Keep copies of all communications** – emails, texts, letters, and receipts. 3. **Document maintenance requests** – take photos, note dates, and keep written responses. 4. **Know the notice periods** – 30 days for rent increases, 24 hours for entry, 10 days for eviction notices. 5. **Report problems early** – give the landlord written notice of any habitability issues. 6. **Seek help if needed** – contact local tenant‑rights groups, HUD, or a lawyer. --- #### Resources | Resource | What it offers | How to access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Information on landlord‑tenant disputes, consumer rights. | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Fair housing complaints, tenant education. | https://www.hud.gov/ | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Discrimination complaints. | https://www.tchra.org/ | | **Local Legal Aid Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance. | Search “legal aid Texas” online. | | **Texas Property Code (Title 2, Chapter 91)** | Full statutory text. | https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/PC/htm/PC.91.htm | If you have a specific scenario—such as a lease dispute, a landlord refusing to make repairs, or a potential eviction—feel free to share more details. I can then offer tailored advice or draft a sample letter or notice that you might send to your landlord.
message.reasoning: The user asks: "What are my rights as a tenant in the state of Texas?" They want information about tenant rights. We can provide general info. But we might also ask clarifying question: Are they looking for a specific type of contract? The tool is for generating contracts. The user didn't request a contract. So we don't need to call the function. Just answer. Provide overview: security deposit limits, notice requirements, habitability, eviction process, etc. Also mention resources. Provide citations? Not required. Just give general info.
